title: This
body:
`this` is decided **at call time, by how the function was called**, not by where it was
written. Four call patterns, four answers.

| Called as | `this` is |
|---|---|
| `foo()` | the global object (`window`), or `undefined` in strict mode |
| `obj.foo()` | `obj`, the thing before the dot |
| `new Foo()` | the newly created object |
| `foo.call(x)` / `.apply(x)` / `.bind(x)` | whatever you passed |

The dot is doing the work. Detach a method from its object and the binding is lost:

```js
const c = { name: "Fred", show() { alert(this.name); } };
c.show();                       // "Fred"
const f = c.show;
f();                            // undefined: called plainly, no dot
```

## In constructor functions

This is what [[Constructor Functions]] rely on. `new` creates an empty object and points
`this` at it:

```js
function Customer(name) { this.name = name; }
const c1 = new Customer("Fred");   // this is the new object
const c2 = Customer("Fred");       // this is the GLOBAL object
```

Forgetting `new` is a silent failure: `c2` is `undefined` and you have quietly added a `name`
property to `window`. That is a [[Logic Errors|logic error]] rather than anything the engine
complains about.

## In event handlers

```js
li.addEventListener("click", function () { this.textContent; });   // this is the li
li.addEventListener("click", () => { this.textContent; });         // this is NOT the li
```

A `function` handler is called by the browser as a method of the node, so `this` is the node.
An [[Arrow Syntax]] handler has no `this` of its own and takes the enclosing scope's, which
at the top level of a script is not the node at all. Use `e.target` from the
[[Event Object]] and the question stops mattering; that is why version 3 in
[[Event Object]] is the preferred one.

## Arrow functions

Arrow functions do not get a `this`. They inherit the one from where they were **defined**,
which is [[Lexical]] `this`, the same rule that produces a [[Closure]]. That makes them
correct inside a method that has a callback in it, and useless as a constructor:

```js
const Bad = (name) => { this.name = name; };
new Bad("Fred");    // TypeError: Bad is not a constructor
```

For the same reason an arrow function cannot be a method on an object literal if it needs
`this` to mean that object. See [[Arrow Syntax]] and [[React]], where lexical `this` is the
behaviour you want.
